transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: okay everybody, good morning, thanks for joining. we wanna do a deep dive on throughput tuning for your PoC with Redwood, mainly continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs and token limits.
[00:12] Tom Rivera: morning, yep this is Tom. quick note, our traffic is a mix of short user prompts and longer system prompts, fairly bursty during peak hours.
[00:20] Jason Liu: great, that's exactly why we wanna look at packing and max_num_seqs, because if you have a lot of short seqs we can pack more into a single batch.
[00:29] Aisha Khan: quick Q — how does Redwood handle KV cache in a multi-tenant burst? we worry about cold-starts and blowing the cache.
[00:36] Priya Kaur: (overlap) and also in VPC mode does cache live on host or in kernel? i saw some notes about K-V cash in the docs, spelled odd.
[00:45] Jason Liu: yeah, good questions. short answer: KV cache is local to the serving process / GPU, it's kept in shared pinned memory for low latency. the tricky bit is cache lifecycle on continuous batching warmup — when there's a sudden tenant change you can see higher misses.
[00:58] Ben Ortiz: miss you say, as in more tokens generated because of miss overhead? or are we seeing latency spike?
[01:05] Jason Liu: both, a cache miss often causes extra kv loads and kernel invocations which bump p95/p99. we mitigate with pre-warming heuristics, sticky routing and a small LRU window for recently used sequences.
[01:17] Tom Rivera: can you explain scheduler knobs? we saw config options but not sure which to change.
[01:23] Jason Liu: sure: there are several we typically tweak — global_max_batch_size, max_num_seqs (packing density), max_tokens_per_batch, and scheduler fairness/window size. by default we bias slightly toward latency, but you can shift to throughput by increasing max_tokens_per_batch and the window so more requests aggregate.
[01:42] Maya Patel: i'll throw up a quick config example in chat after, but conceptually think of it as tradeoff: more batching = higher throughput and lower token cost, but tail latency increases unless you tune windows and timeouts.
[01:55] Aisha Khan: what's a recommended starting point for max_num_seqs? our average seq length is 64 tokens, 20% are 200+ tokens.
[02:03] Jason Liu: start at 16 for mixed workloads, 32 if you mostly have short sequences under 128. with 64 average you'd get diminishing returns packing beyond 32 because of padding overhead.
[02:14] Tom Rivera: and continuous batching warmup — how long till it's stable? we ran a test and saw throughput ramp for 10-15 minutes.
[02:22] Priya Kaur: we hit a weird oscillation where throughput dropped at minute 12 and then came back.
[02:27] Jason Liu: oscillation usually implies the scheduler window is too small and the autoscaler is reacting; or the cache thrashing because tenants redirect to different hosts. for warmup expect ~5-20 minutes depending on traffic volatility; longer for very bursty loads.
[02:40] Ben Ortiz: any knobs to reduce oscillation?
[02:43] Jason Liu: increase scheduler window, increase min_batch_fill_time (we call it batching_delay_ms), and tune autoscaler cooldowns. also set a sticky routing policy for the same session ids so the KV hits improve.
[02:55] Tom Rivera: we saw recommendations about max tokens per request. do we need to cap user tokens?
[03:00] Jason Liu: yes, we often put per-request token limits to avoid one long tail request blocking batches. you can enforce max_input_tokens or max_total_tokens; another pattern is to place longer jobs on a dedicated pool (dedicated capacity) so hosted pool stays low-latency.
[03:16] Aisha Khan: what's the impact of quantization on throughput vs accuracy? we tested 4-bit quant and saw big perf but slight regressions in few-shot.
[03:24] Jason Liu: quantization is a powerful lever — 4-bit/8-bit can reduce inference memory and improve throughput. tradeoff is sometimes quality drift, particularly for complex instructions. our recommendation: run a QA-eval set on your prompts with candidate quant configs. often 4-bit with targeted fp16 for attention gives good perf with minimal regressions.
[03:42] Maya Patel: we have a shared benchmark sheet and a small eval harness - i'll link it right after.
[03:46] Tom Rivera: perfect, please include the exact commands / config for scheduler knobs.
[03:50] Priya Kaur: i also want to know about metrics to watch — what should we graph?
[03:55] Jason Liu: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, batch_size_histogram, kv_cache_hit_rate, gpu_utilization per device, kernel-launch rate, and queue length. also watch per-tenant collision metrics for multi-tenant.
[04:10] Aisha Khan: can you show an example config for heavy-throughput bias?
[04:13] Jason Liu: yeah, here's an example i typed in chat (paraphrased):
  scheduler: {
    bias: throughput,
    scheduler_window_ms: 120,
    batching_delay_ms: 30,
    global_max_batch_size: 512,
    max_num_seqs: 32,
    max_tokens_per_batch: 32768
  }
[04:34] Ben Ortiz: those numbers seem big — global_max_batch_size 512, are we not limited by GPU mem?
[04:39] Jason Liu: it's logical max; runtime enforces memory-safe packing. global_max_batch_size is mostly an upper bound across devices; per-GPU actual-packed batch is lower depending on seq lengths and quant. we also have memory-based runtime checks.
[04:51] Tom Rivera: about VPC/on-prem: any differences to expect on latency for private deployments? we plan to run private in our cloud connected VPC.
[04:59] Jason Liu: network egress within VPC is low-latency but watch your NAT and egress rules if you route telemetry. more importantly on-prem or air-gapped we run the same runtime but you need to tune for network-attached storage vs local NVMe for model cache. KV cache stays local to the GPU process though.
[05:16] Priya Kaur: will the autoscaler behave differently in Private mode?
[05:19] Jason Liu: autoscaler logic is the same but the triggers differ — private installs often have reserved capacity and different policies; you'll want more conservative scale-in cooldowns to avoid oscillation.
[05:28] Aisha Khan: curious about metrics during quant runs — does kernel launch rate change significantly?
[05:33] Jason Liu: yes, quantized kernels often reduce compute but may increase kernel-launch density due to packing; we observed a 1.2x-1.8x improvement in tokens/sec in our internal bench on similar models. p99 sometimes regresses slightly if attention kernels are slower in certain seq lengths.
[05:51] Tom Rivera: can Redwood route to a fallback model when a quantized variant misses quality threshold?
[05:56] Maya Patel: absolutely, we support automated fallback policies — routing by model family and confidence. you can do canary rollouts from quant to fp16 and set a percentage or quality gate.
[06:07] Ben Ortiz: what's the recommended approach for mixed workloads: dedicated pool for long jobs and hosted pool for short jobs?
[06:13] Jason Liu: yes that's common. put chatty, low-latency traffic on the low-quant, highly optimized pool; put batchy long-run jobs on dedicated or dedicated GPU shards with relaxed latency SLOs.
[06:23] Aisha Khan: regarding bench results, you mentioned earlier that we should expect warmup 5-20 minutes. what should baseline throughput look like?
[06:31] Jason Liu: depends on model and quant: for a Llama-2-13B-like model on A100s with 4-bit we commonly see 10-30k tokens/sec per GPU with packing; with no packing that drops to 3-8k tokens/sec. numbers are noisy, so that's why the 48-hour run is useful.
[06:49] Tom Rivera: we've got mixed hardware across our internal cluster, some A10s and older V100s — how to handle hetero clusters?
[06:57] Jason Liu: smart routing helps — route by hardware profile, or segment pools by hw type. avoid packing across hetero devices; runtime will not pack across incompatible GPUs.
[07:08] Priya Kaur: question on max_num_seqs: does it refer to maximum sequences per batch or per GPU?
[07:13] Jason Liu: it's per-packed-batch (the algorithm attempts to pack up to max_num_seqs into a single packed batch), and then mapping to GPU happens; effective per-GPU count depends on packing and device mapping.
[07:24] Ben Ortiz: any gotchas with rate limiting + batching?
[07:28] Jason Liu: you can end up with head-of-line blocking if a big request is allowed and smaller ones are queued behind it; enforce per-request token caps or split large jobs into background pools. also separate token-based quotas vs requests-per-minute to avoid quota starvation during bursts.
[07:46] Aisha Khan: earlier you mentioned kernel selection — can we pin kernels or force a kernel family?
[07:51] Jason Liu: runtime picks kernels based on model architecture and seq length distribution; we expose an advanced flag to prefer low-latency kernels at the cost of throughput or vice versa. use this only after benchmarking.
[08:02] Tom Rivera: can we see a sample run report? we had an internal doc but want Redwood's format.
[08:07] Maya Patel: yes i'll attach the benchmark spreadsheet; it includes p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, batch histograms, kv hit, kernel launch rate.
[08:15] Jason Liu: one more tip: if your traffic has a heavy tail of long prompts, try multi-tier routing — short prompts to a high-concurrency pool with high packing, long prompts to a lower concurrency dedicated pool.
[08:26] Ben Ortiz: ok that sounds like a plan.
[08:29] Tom Rivera: side question — for compliance we need audit logs and kms integration in Private, is there any perf hit for encryption?
[08:36] Maya Patel: minimal for in-flight TLS; KMS for key retrieval is once at startup or per-rotation. if you use HSM for per-request signing that's different but uncommon. Private supports KMS/HSM integrations and we can provide the security docs.
[08:49] Aisha Khan: any recommended default knob set we should try for initial test?
[08:52] Jason Liu: try: max_num_seqs=32, scheduler_window_ms=100-120, batching_delay_ms=25-40, max_tokens_per_batch=32768, global_max_batch_size=512, quant=4-bit (eval first). Use sticky routing session_id hashing.
[09:08] Priya Kaur: we will provide prompt distribution; is there a preferred format?
[09:12] Jason Liu: csv with columns session_id, seq_len, prompt_sample, timestamp, percentile bucket. that works.
[09:19] Tom Rivera: let's recap next steps.
[09:22] Maya Patel: recap: Redwood runs 48-hour throughput test with the above config and shares the raw perf logs; BrightScale will provide traffic distribution and prompt set; Redwood shares tuning guide + benchmark sheet and runbook; schedule follow-up to review results.
[09:38] Ben Ortiz: sounds good. thanks.
[09:41] Tom Rivera: thanks everyone.
[09:42] Maya Patel: thanks, we'll send the links and configs after the call.
[09:46] (meeting ends)
